title: Understanding Public Budgets
tagline: Where public money comes from, how it is decided, and how to follow it.
description: Public money pays for clinics, schools, roads and boreholes. It comes from all of us, through taxes. This course explains where government money comes from, how the national budget and CDF are decided, and how you can follow the money and ask good questions about how it is spent in your community.
outcomes: Name the main sources of public money
Describe what government spends money on
Explain the yearly budget cycle and Parliament's role
Explain how the Constituency Development Fund works
Use the Auditor General's reports and project information
Ask clear questions about public spending

modules.title: Where public money comes from
modules.summary: Taxes, other income, borrowing and what it pays for.

lessons.title: Where public money comes from
lessons.body:
Government does not have its own money. **Public money** is collected from people and businesses, and from other sources, to pay for services everyone shares.

## Taxes
Most public money comes from **taxes**, collected by the **Zambia Revenue Authority (ZRA)**:

- **Pay As You Earn (PAYE):** taken from workers' salaries.
- **Value Added Tax (VAT):** included in the price of many goods and services you buy.
- **Company taxes** on business profits.
- **Mineral royalties** paid by mining companies.
- **Customs and excise duties** on imports and on goods like fuel, alcohol and airtime.

Even if you do not earn a salary, you pay taxes when you buy goods. Public money is **your money too**.

## Other income
- **Fees and levies**, such as for licences, permits and passports.
- **Council revenue**: market levies, business levies and property rates, which stay with your council.
- **Grants** from other countries and international organisations.

## Borrowing
When income is not enough, government **borrows**, from lenders inside Zambia and abroad. Borrowed money must be paid back with interest.

## Why it matters
Because public money comes from citizens, citizens have the right to know how it is spent, and to ask questions when it is not spent well.
key_points: Most public money comes from taxes collected by ZRA
You pay tax, like VAT, when you shop
Public money is citizens' money
lessons.try_it: Look at a shop receipt and see whether VAT is shown.

lessons.title: What public money pays for
lessons.body:
The national budget shares public money between many needs. Each year, government decides how much goes where.

## Main areas of spending
- **Education:** teachers' salaries, schools, bursaries and free education.
- **Health:** clinics, hospitals, medicines and health workers.
- **Agriculture:** support to farmers, such as inputs and extension services.
- **Social protection:** support for the poorest households, such as the **social cash transfer**.
- **Roads, bridges and energy.**
- **Water and sanitation.**
- **Local government:** money to councils and the **Constituency Development Fund (CDF)**.
- **Security and justice:** police, defence, courts and prisons.
- **Salaries and running costs** of government.
- **Debt repayment:** paying back loans with interest.

## Recurrent and capital spending
- **Recurrent spending** happens every year: salaries, medicines, fuel, electricity bills.
- **Capital spending** builds things that last: a new school, a road, a bridge.

Both matter. A new clinic (capital) is not useful without nurses and medicines (recurrent).

## Trade-offs
Money is limited. More for roads may mean less for something else. That is why the budget is debated, and why citizens' views matter.

## What reaches your area
National figures are large. What matters most is whether services actually arrive in your community, on time and in good condition.
key_points: Spending is shared between many needs
Recurrent spending repeats; capital spending builds
Money is limited, so choices must be made
lessons.try_it: Name one public service in your area and whether it is mostly recurrent or capital spending.

lessons.title: Borrowing and public debt
lessons.body:
Like a family that takes a loan to build a house, government sometimes borrows to pay for big projects or when income falls short.

## Where government borrows
- **Domestic borrowing:** from banks, pension funds and investors in Zambia, through **government bonds** and **Treasury bills**.
- **External borrowing:** from other countries, international lenders such as the World Bank and the IMF, and private investors abroad.

## Why debt matters to you
Borrowed money must be paid back with **interest**. Every kwacha spent on debt repayment is a kwacha that cannot go to clinics or schools that year. If debt grows too large, repayments can squeeze out important services.

Zambia went through a difficult debt period in recent years, and has worked with its lenders to **restructure** its debt, meaning to agree new repayment terms.

## Good and bad borrowing
Borrowing can be useful when it pays for projects that help the economy grow, like roads that help farmers reach markets, or electricity that lets businesses work. It is risky when it pays for projects that are overpriced, poorly built or never finished.

## Questions citizens can ask
- What is this loan for?
- How much will it cost to repay, and over how long?
- Is the project finished, and is it working?

Information on public debt is published by the **Ministry of Finance and National Planning** and discussed in Parliament.
key_points: Borrowed money must be repaid with interest
Debt repayments reduce money for services
Ask what a loan is for and whether the project works
lessons.try_it: Find one news story about Zambia's public debt from a trusted source.

modules.title: How the budget is decided
modules.summary: The budget cycle, reading budget numbers and CDF.

lessons.title: The yearly budget cycle
lessons.body:
Zambia's government budget covers one **financial year**, from **January to December**. Preparing, approving and checking it is a cycle that runs all year.

## 1. Planning
Ministries and public bodies say what they need for the coming year, based on national development plans. The **Ministry of Finance and National Planning** sets limits. It also holds **pre-budget consultations**, where organisations and the public can send views.

## 2. The budget speech
Usually around **late September**, the **Minister of Finance** presents the budget to the **National Assembly** in the **budget speech**. It explains planned income, spending and tax changes. Detailed figures are published in the **Estimates of Revenue and Expenditure**, often called the **Yellow Book**.

## 3. Approval by Parliament
MPs debate the budget. Committees examine each ministry's spending plans. Parliament then passes an **Appropriation Act**, which gives legal authority to spend the money. Government should not spend public money without Parliament's approval.

## 4. Spending
From January, the **Treasury** releases money to ministries, provinces and councils, who carry out the plans.

## 5. Checking
The **Auditor General** audits how money was spent and reports to Parliament. Parliament's **Public Accounts Committee** examines those reports and questions officials.

## Where you come in
You can send views during consultations, listen to the budget speech, talk to your MP before the vote, and follow up on spending in your area. The **Planning and Budgeting Act of 2020** sets out how planning and budgeting should work.
key_points: The financial year runs January to December
The budget is presented to Parliament around late September
Parliament approves spending through an Appropriation Act
lessons.try_it: Listen to part of the next budget speech, or read a news summary of it.

lessons.title: Making sense of budget numbers
lessons.body:
Budget figures are huge and can be confusing. A few simple tricks help.

## Millions and billions
- **1 million** = 1,000,000 (one thousand thousand).
- **1 billion** = 1,000,000,000 (one thousand million).

So K1.5 billion is K1,500 million. When you hear figures on the radio, listen for million or billion. It makes a thousand-fold difference.

## Per person
Big numbers become clearer when you divide them. Zambia has around 20 million people. If a programme gets K200 million, that is about **K10 per person** across the country. If you know how many pupils, patients or households a programme serves, you can work out what each one receives.

## Share of the total
Compare a sector with the whole budget. If health gets 10 out of every 100 kwacha, that is **10%**. Watching whether this share goes up or down over years tells you about government priorities.

## Allocated versus released versus spent
- **Allocated:** the amount in the approved budget.
- **Released:** what the Treasury actually sends.
- **Spent:** what was used.

These can be very different. A road may be in the budget for years but receive little money. Ask: *how much was actually released?*

## Inflation
If prices rise by 10% in a year, a budget that grows by only 5% can buy **less** than before. Keep this in mind when you hear that a budget "increased".
key_points: 1 billion is 1,000 million
Divide by people served to understand big numbers
Allocated, released and spent are not the same
lessons.try_it: Take one budget figure from the news and work out roughly how much it is per person.

lessons.title: Local money: councils and CDF
lessons.body:
Not all public money is decided in Lusaka. Some is decided close to you.

## Council budgets
Each council prepares its own budget, using its own income (levies, fees, rates) and money from national government. Council meetings that discuss the budget are generally open to the public.

## The Constituency Development Fund (CDF)
**CDF** is money given to every constituency each year for local development. The amount is set in the national budget and has grown a lot since 2021. It is managed under the **Constituency Development Fund Act** through the council, with a **CDF committee** in each constituency.

CDF is used for:

- **Community projects**, such as classrooms, boreholes, health posts, bridges and markets.
- **Empowerment**: grants and loans for cooperatives, clubs and small businesses, with priority for women and youth.
- **Secondary boarding school bursaries** for pupils who cannot afford fees.
- **Skills development bursaries** for training at skills and trades institutions.

## How projects are chosen
Communities propose projects, often through **Ward Development Committees**. The CDF committee reviews them, and the council and ministry approve them. Calls for applications for bursaries and empowerment are advertised by councils, usually with deadlines.

## How to apply
Watch for adverts from your council and on its official page, and ask your councillor or the council's CDF office for application forms and deadlines. Applications are free. Be careful of anyone asking for money to "help" you get CDF.
key_points: CDF funds local projects, empowerment and bursaries
Each constituency has a CDF committee
Applying is free; ask your council for forms
lessons.try_it: Ask your councillor when the next CDF applications open.

modules.title: Following the money
modules.summary: Audits, tracking projects and asking good questions.

lessons.title: The Auditor General and Parliament
lessons.body:
After money is spent, someone must check whether it was used properly. That is the job of the **Office of the Auditor General**.

## What the Auditor General does
The Auditor General is independent and checks the accounts of ministries, provinces, councils and many public bodies. Each year, the Office reports to Parliament on problems found, such as:

- money spent without proper approval,
- payments for goods or works never delivered,
- missing documents for spending,
- unfinished or poor-quality projects,
- money not collected that should have been.

## What happens next
Parliament's **Public Accounts Committee** examines the reports, calls officials to explain, and makes recommendations. Serious cases may be referred to bodies such as the **Anti-Corruption Commission** or the police.

## Reading the reports
Auditor General reports are public. They are published on the Office's official website and are often covered in the news. They are long, but you can search them for your **district**, **council** or a **project** you know.

## Why this matters
Audits show where systems are weak. Citizens, journalists and civil society organisations use them to ask questions and push for action. Over time, this pressure can improve how public money is managed.

## Remember
An audit finding is a reason to ask questions, not proof that a specific person stole money. Problems can also come from poor record-keeping or delays.
key_points: The Auditor General independently checks public spending
The Public Accounts Committee questions officials
Audit reports are public and can be searched
lessons.try_it: Search the latest Auditor General report for your district's name.

lessons.title: Asking good questions about spending
lessons.body:
You do not need to be an accountant to follow public money. Good questions are enough.

## Start with what you can see
Look at projects in your area: a school block, a borehole, a road, a clinic. Ask:

- **What** is being built or provided?
- **Who** is responsible: which council, ministry or contractor?
- **How much** was budgeted, and how much has been spent?
- **When** should it be finished?
- **Is it working** as promised, and is the quality good?

## Look for project boards
Many public projects display a **notice board** showing the project name, funding source (such as CDF), contractor, cost and dates. Take a photo of it. If there is no board, ask why.

## Ask in the right places
- **Your councillor** and **Ward Development Committee** for local and CDF projects.
- **The council's** officers, such as the CDF office or planning office.
- **Your MP's office.**
- **Public meetings**, such as council meetings and budget consultations.

## Use your right to information
Under the **Access to Information Act of 2023**, you can request information such as contract details and spending reports from public bodies. The course *Your Right to Information* explains how.

## Keep it respectful and factual
Write down answers, dates and names. Share findings honestly, separating what you saw from what you suspect.
key_points: Ask what, who, how much, when, and is it working
Photograph project notice boards
Request information formally when needed
lessons.try_it: Find a public project near you and note what its notice board says.

lessons.title: Practice: tracking a local project
lessons.body:
Let us follow an example.

*A new classroom block at Mwanawasa Primary School was announced 18 months ago, funded by CDF. The walls are up, but there is no roof, and work has stopped.*

## Step 1: Gather what you know
Visit the site. Take dated photos. Note what is finished and what is not. Photograph the **project board**: it shows the contractor, the cost, the start date and the planned completion date.

## Step 2: Ask locally
Talk to the head teacher and the school's parent-teacher association. Then ask your **councillor** or **Ward Development Committee**: *Why has work stopped? Has the contractor been paid? When will work continue?*

## Step 3: Ask the council
Visit or write to the council's **CDF office**. Ask politely for the contract value, the amounts paid so far, and the current plan. Keep a copy of your letter and note the date.

## Step 4: Use formal channels if needed
If you get no answer, make a request under the **Access to Information Act**. You can also contact your **MP's office**.

## Step 5: Share and follow up
Share what you learned, with facts and photos, in a community meeting or with local media. Follow up every few weeks.

## Possible outcomes
Often there is a simple reason, like funds not yet released or a contractor problem, and attention helps solve it. If you find signs of corruption, report them to the **Anti-Corruption Commission** with your evidence.
key_points: Start with facts and photos
Ask locally, then the council, then formally
Report signs of corruption to the ACC
lessons.try_it: Choose one project in your area and write three questions you would ask about it.

lessons.title: Final check: Understanding public budgets
lessons.body: Questions covering the whole course. Score 70% or more to complete it. You can try again as many times as you like.

quiz.question: Who independently checks how public money was spent?
quiz.explanation: The Auditor General audits and reports to Parliament.

options: So you can track the project and ask informed questions
It is required by law for citizens
quiz.explanation: The board gives facts you can follow up.

quiz.question: Which law lets you request information like contract details from public bodies?
quiz.explanation: The Access to Information Act gives a right to request information.

quiz.question: What are three ways CDF is used?
quiz.explanation: CDF funds projects, empowerment grants and loans, and bursaries.

quiz.question: A road has K10 million allocated but only K2 million released. What does this tell you?
options: Most of the planned money has not yet reached the project
